podcast.title: Screaming Fist (May 1977) – Possible First Canadian Punk Vinyl; Song Named William Gibson's Operation in Neuromancer
podcast.body: The Viletones formed in Toronto in December 1976 and were at the Ramones' first Toronto show on September 26, 1976. They released a three-track, seven-inch single possibly as early as May 1977, making them contenders for the first Canadian band on vinyl. The key track is called "Screaming Fist." Science fiction writer William Gibson later named a fictional covert operation in his landmark 1984 novel *Neuromancer* — in which hackers attack Soviet infrastructure — "Operation Screaming Fist," directly after the Viletones song. Gibson also coined the term "cyberspace" two years prior. "Gibson was also the person who first coined the term cyberspace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Canadian Punk Band
podcast.body: The Vyletones are noted as one of the fiercest early Canadian punk bands. "Canada's Vyletones, one of the fiercest of the early Canadian punk bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Knife Purchase with Sid Vicious
podcast.body: Steve Lucky, a member of the Canadian band The Viletones, accompanied Sid Vicious when he purchased the 007 hunting knife on 42nd Street that would later be used in Nancy Spungen's murder. "Sid had bought it with a couple of friends, including Steve Lucky of the Canadian band The Vile Tones at a place on 42nd Street."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Steve Lucky's Commentary on Sid Vicious – Foreshadowed Death
podcast.body: Steve Lucky, a member of the Canadian band The Vialtoons, was present when Sid Vicious purchased the knife later implicated in Nancy Spungen's death. He commented that Sid's death was unsurprising and "bathed in banality," as Sid "really did give off the vibe that he really clearly was not fully here." "Sid was bathed in benality. You know, and you could see it coming a mile away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Toronto Origins and Road Trip
podcast.body: The Vial Tones traveled from Toronto to play in New York, reportedly robbing gas stations along their route. "There were the vial tones who had made the trip down from Toronto, apparently robbing gas stations on their way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Possible First All-Female Canadian Punk Band; Shoeshine Boy Written About Emanuel Jaques Murder (1977)
xref.body: The Curse are contenders with the B-Girls for the title of Canada's first all-female punk band, having been ready to perform as early as May 1977. The following month they played CBGB in New York on a bill with the Viletones, Diodes, and Teenage Head. They were more intense than the B-Girls — member Mickey Skin performed with a fake lobotomy scar and the band had an explicitly feminist agenda, often starting food fights at shows. Their most controversial song, "Shoeshine Boy," was written about the 1977 murder of 12-year-old Emanuel Jaques in Toronto: a boy shining shoes on Yonge Street who was offered $35 to help move photographic equipment, then tortured and raped for 12 hours before being strangled and drowned in a kitchen sink. The crime catalyzed the city's cleanup of its red-light district. "They were intent on destroying the patriarchy of music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York City (1979) – Genuine Canadian Punk Classic About Toronto Bands Making Road Trips to CBGB
xref.body: The Demics formed in London, Ontario in 1977 and regularly made the drive to Toronto to participate in the scene. Drummer Marcy Saddy later left to join the B-Girls. Their EP *Talk's Cheap* appeared in 1978 on Toronto's Ready Records, followed by an album in 1980. Their best-known song, "New York City," is a tribute to the Toronto punk bands — the Viletones, the B-Girls, the Curse, the Diodes, and others — who would regularly drive nine hours to New York City to play CBGB and couch-surf. "The song is about those Toronto bands that would regularly drive the nine hours to New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Friends with Blondie and Ramones; Almost Signed to IRS; Influenced B-52s; Background Vocals on Blondie's Autoamerican
xref.body: The B-Girls formed in Toronto in 1977 with a sound closer to British Invasion mid-1960s than hard punk, though their look and attitude were fully punk. They toured with and opened for Teenage Head, the Viletones, and eventually The Clash, then relocated to New York where they became close with Blondie, the Ramones, the Cramps, and the Dead Boys. Members sang background vocals on Blondie's *Autoamerican* (1980), had demos produced by Debbie Harry and Mick Jones of The Clash, and nearly signed with IRS Records — which chose a Los Angeles band called the Go-Go's instead. The Go-Go's were fans of the B-Girls. The B-Girls' existence and sound also influenced a band from Georgia called the B-52s. No album was released before the original lineup fell apart by 1981. "This Canadian punk band influenced not just Blondie and the Go-Go's, but a band visiting New York from Georgia called the B-52s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
